Emergency responders gather after a shooting on November 7, 2026 in the main aarket square of Krakow, Poland [Omar Marques/Getty Images]By AFP, AP and ReutersPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Five people have been killed and others wounded in a shooting near the main ‌‌market square of Krakow in southern Poland, police said.
“As a result of the incident, five people were killed and around a dozen others were wounded,” a Krakow police spokesperson told the AFP news agency on Saturday.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Three injured in third school attack in Poland in less than a weeklist 2 of 3Polish police deployed to top court after head judge suspendedlist 3 of 3Poland’s president joins protest amid constitutional crisis at top courtend of list
He added that the gunman was “neutralised” by police officers and transported to hospital.
A man was firing toward random people from a car driving through the city’s Main Square, Krakow police told the Associated Press, confirming the death toll. Police officers are among the wounded.
Krakow’s municipal government said earlier on X that deaths and injuries were reported after shots were fired in a square in Poland’s second-largest city, without adding details.
A “tragic shooting” took place on Saturday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a post on X.
“I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow,” he wrote, adding that “the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack”.
Krakow is about 250 kilometres (155 miles) south of the capital, Warsaw.

item.title: The Lions by the River Tigris: Restoring Mosul’s artefacts
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration play-arrow
When the ancient Iraqi city of Mosul is devastated after liberation from ISIL, three men strive to revive its beauty.Read more
In the heart of war-ravaged Mosul, two carved lions stand as a fragile link to the city’s shattered past. Bashar, a fisherman, lost his once-grand family home during the battle to liberate the city from ISIL (ISIS) nearly 10 years ago. All that remains is a marble gate crowned with lions, which he fiercely guards.
Fakhri, a devoted collector determined to save Mosul’s heritage, becomes obsessed with acquiring the lions gate for his unofficial museum. His friend Fadil, a musician once silenced under ISIL, challenges him to see the human cost behind every artefact. As Mosul rebuilds, a quiet cultural revival reflects the resilience of a city with 8,000 years of history.
The Lions by the River Tigris is a documentary film by Zaradasht Ahmed.Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026

Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein [File:Ahmed Saad/Reuters] (Reuters)By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Iraq has evidence that external parties have been using its territory to launch attacks on neighbouring countries, its foreign minister told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview on Saturday.
Baghdad is investigating attacks launched from Iraqi territory against Gulf states and is seeking to resolve disagreements with Saudi Arabia through dialogue, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Iraq’s PM tells Saudi crown prince Iraqi territory will not be used for attackslist 2 of 3Iraq parliament approves al-Zaidi’s cabinet amid growing economic concernslist 3 of 3Iraq’s al-Zaidi talks to Trump as Baghdad seeks to stay out of war on Iranend of list
Saudi Arabia has accused Iran-aligned groups operating in Iraq of attacking its oil infrastructure. In September, Baghdad confirmed that drone attacks on the kingdom’s East-West pipeline originated from Iraqi territory.
Hussein told Al Jazeera that Baghdad was negotiating with Iran-aligned armed factions to bring their weapons under state control and the process must be pursued through dialogue rather than force.
He also said Iraq was in contact with Tehran regarding the issue of weapons held by Iraqi factions.
Iraq’s government had initially established a deadline for armed factions to bring their weapons under state control by September 30, when the US-led international coalition to combat ISIL (ISIS) was set to end their mandate and leave the country.
However, it pushed back the deadline to June 2027 after encountering resistance to the policy, despite long-standing pressure from the US to fulfil its disarmament pledge.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become speaker of the House, speaks at a news conference in Washington, DC, on November 4, 2026 [J Scott Applewhite/AP Photo]By Tamara KhandakerPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
With Democrats’ decisive victory in the United States’ midterm elections on Tuesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York is on the verge of making history as the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives.
For the 56-year-old congressman, it would be the culmination of almost two decades in office, giving him a central role in Democrats’ efforts to rein in Republican US President Donald Trump in the final two years of his presidency.

But as Jeffries celebrated the “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats back into power the day after the election, some within the party were not convinced that the congressman, known for his cautious approach to politics and longstanding support for Israel, was the right man for the moment.
An online petition on Change.org calling on lawmakers to choose another speaker had collected more than 980,000 signatures by Saturday morning, while several newly elected progressive lawmakers have not said whether they will support him.
“We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” the petition reads.
“This is not a foregone conclusion,” it continues, urging others to run for the job.

Hard-left French leader Jean-Luc Melenchon has been described as a “radical” by right-wing opponents, a “despot” by former allies and a “hero” by some of the students who have taken to the streets in nationwide protests.
The leader of the France Unbowed (LFI) party has emerged as the strongest contender on the left and potential challenger to far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential election.

On Saturday, Melenchon is presenting his programme at a rally in Le Bourget, north of Paris, a day after it was published online.
Among his proposals, he wants to lower the retirement age to 60 and raise the minimum wage to 1,700 euro ($1,900) a month; pull France out of NATO and renationalise parts of the economy.
He wants the European Central Bank to stop France repaying the debt it holds, effectively transforming the debt instead to a permanent interest-free loan – a move he hopes would give the government more room to spend.
On Europe, he envisions France remaining in the EU, but he wants to refuse rules that conflict with the nation’s social, environmental or economic programmes, setting up a potentially confrontational relationship with Brussels.

Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine – There are only eight people left in Volodymyr’s village. That was the last count he remembers before deciding to leave.
“We were in the cellar when they started bombing us with drones,” he said, nervously rubbing his red, blistered hands together. “As you can see, I was completely burned.”

He and his neighbours sheltered in a basement to escape. He said the attack ultimately prompted him to evacuate [George Llewelyn/Al Jazeera]
The villages south of Zaporizhzhia have been coming under escalating Russian attacks.
On November 2, in one of this year’s deadliest attacks in Ukraine, nine Russian glide bombs struck the town of Komyshuvakha, killing at least 50 people. Many had gathered to receive humanitarian aid at a local school. Several people are still missing, feared dead under the rubble.

Floods have drenched large areas of Gaza [Lina Ghassan Abu Zayed/Al Jazeera]By Lina Ghassan Abu ZayedPublished On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.
Hmeida, her husband and children have been awake since midnight as heavy rain and strong winds swept through the camp. Water seeped into the tent and drenched their belongings. With all their clothes wet, Hmeida had to ask neighbours to help dry their clothes.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How Israel is tightening its grip on Palestinian schools in East Jerusalemlist 2 of 3Palestinian citizens of Israel put to ‘loyalty test’ after election winslist 3 of 3Rains flood 70,000 displaced families’ tents in Gazaend of list
“Since midnight, we have been sitting awake. Water came into our tent, and the bedding, blankets and everything else got soaked. In the morning, I found my son and little daughter shivering. My two-month-old baby was freezing,” Hmeida told Al Jazeera.
“What am I supposed to do? Hold my children or try to stop the water? I was trying to keep them warm while carrying my little girl, but the water kept coming in. The wind was so strong that we felt the tent was about to be ripped out of the ground.”
Her husband, Sameh Hmeida, 30, said the family’s tent is particularly exposed due to its close proximity to the sea. It has no tarpaulins or insulating materials that might have helped in the storm.
